newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Budapest bucks weak trend in east Europe markets.
newsitem.headline: Budapest bucks weak trend in east Europe markets.

text.p: The Budapest stock market stood out in eastern Europe this week with record-breaking gains, while most other markets lost ground.
Warsaw, Prague and Bratislava were all weak and Zagreb closed the week mixed. Strong demand for Slovenian and Romanian blue chips moved markets ahead in Ljubljana and Bucharest.
The Central European Share Index (CESI), which measures price movements in 72 Hungarian, Polish, Czech, Slovak and Slovenian stocks, inched down 1.16 percent to 1,447.01 points.
BUDAPEST

The Budapest bourse set successive record levels this week. Profit-taking and the closing of positions on the futures market trimmed some of the gains on Thursday, but the market's outlook remained basically positive.

An upgrade of Hungary's long-term foreign currency rating to BBB from BBB- by IBCA and the reduction of the monthly crawling peg devaluation to one percent from 1.1 percent starting August 15 drew fresh foreign capital into the market.
WARSAW
Polish shares fell 5.4 percent this week to 15,177.2 points. Analysts saw the market staying flat or falling as it went into July, due to the public offering of copper giant KGHM Polska Miedz.
KGHM's 1.3-1.7-billion-zloty flotation starts on June 30, the same day that Bank Handlowy joins the main market. KGHM starts trading on July 10.

Some analysts said a central banker's warning on Tuesday that Poland faced a Czech-style financial crisis in 1998 due to its widening trade gap was a negative signal. But they added that the finance minister's reply on Wednesday that Poland was ready to tackle the problem could help quell concerns.
PRAGUE
Czech shares slumped in sluggish activity in the week to Thursday with the PX50 index's most heavily capitalised banking issue Komercni Banka losing 10 percent of its value.

Analysts say Komercni's recent string of losses is connected with the Czech central bank's high interest rate regime. This has raised the prospect of increased bad debt problems this year. The discount rate was recently raised to 13.0 percent from 10.5.
Komercni accounts for 11.4 percent of the PX50's total capitalisation.
BRATISLAVA

The Bratislava Stock Exchange fell in listless trading this week, continuing a decline which started in May when the money market was paralysed by foreign speculation. Brokers said an improvement was unlikely in the near future.
The bourse has been also hit by a lack of liquidity as investors, put off by a murky market and political fears, have waited on the sidelines.
The 16-share SAX index fell 3.25 points, or 1.9 percent, to close at 167.45 points on Thursday after a year low of 166.01 points on Wednesday.
LJUBLJANA
Slovenian shares rose 1.38 percent this week, as the blue- chip SBI index drifted up 16.9 points to 1,237.6 on Thursday.
But traders did not expect the uptrend to last in the longer term, anticipating slack business in the summer season.
ZAGREB
Croatian stocks closed mixed on Thursday after brisk activity throughout the week, with blue chip drugs firm Pliva accounting for much of the trade.
Brokers said the market was in a positive cycle.
BUCHAREST
Active buying, mostly by foreigners, helped most Bucharest prices gain on average as well as closing quotes this week.
Three independent market indices, the BIG, the VAB and the CAS-SE, based on average prices and market capitalisation, touched new highs for the year on Thursday.
The first tier, trading seven stocks, took the bulk of the week's turnover level.
